title: Blog — Shubh
text:
Skip to content
← Shubh
Starting a venture fund
↓
Build in public is the worst psyop in the world
↓
Larping and the case of larpers
↓
I recently raised $5 million for a venture fund. I want to use it to back people who come from backgrounds like mine, especially people who are smart and ambitious but do not yet have much money, access, or permission.
I grew up in Bihar and got my first laptop in ninth grade. It was not a great laptop, but it gave me the internet—and the internet gave me a way to learn, build, and find opportunities I could not see around me.
I have met plenty of people who are just as capable, but never got the laptop, introduction, time, or encouragement they needed. Talent is everywhere. Access is not.
So I want to help with the first step: small checks, honest feedback, and practical support. I am especially interested in technically ambitious projects and unusual people who are still early. You do not need a polished pitch. You just need something you care enough to keep working on.
If you are building something cool, email me at
shubh@shubhxho.com
. Tell me what it is, why you care, and what a small amount of money would help you do. I received an Emergent Ventures grant myself, and it gave me the room to work. I want to give someone else a bit of that room.
Back to the index ↑
Build in public is the worst psyop in the world.
I mean the version where you spend more time making sure people know you are building than actually building. The daily update. The screenshot of a dashboard. The thread about what you learned. Eventually, you start choosing work because it will make a good post. A hard problem that takes three quiet weeks begins to feel like a bad investment.
That is a ridiculous way to get good at anything. You can become excellent at looking like a builder without developing the ability to build much.
I still want to learn in public. If I figure something out, I want to explain it. If I get something wrong, I want someone who understands it better to tell me. A technical write-up can start a conversation I would never have had otherwise. Publishing the work has a real purpose.
The order matters, though. I want the work to determine what I publish, not a posting schedule to determine what I work on.
The uncomfortable part is that attention does matter. A good project can introduce me to a collaborator, a mentor, or someone who will back a more ambitious idea later. Pretending distribution is beneath me is just another way to avoid doing something difficult.
So I need a better rule than “build in public.” Build quickly, learn something real, and use the finished work to find people worth building with. This is the thesis I want to operate from.
Use attention as infrastructure
The mission is to become prepared and resourced to start a generational company as quickly as possible.
That means becoming capable enough to build it and finding people who would want to build it with me. Attention is useful when it helps those two things happen. An audience on its own is not progress; it is just a number I can look at.
Get technical. Find our people.
Identify the next technology wave and learn the stacks that let me work on it. Get past the demo. Understand what breaks, what costs too much, and what is suddenly possible that was not possible a year ago.
Find exceptional builders and mentors. Make something worth showing them. Ask specific questions, follow through on the advice, and come back with results. The fastest way to get close to good people is to do useful work with them.
Maintain those relationships actively. Remember what people are working on. Send something useful. Help when I can. I do not want a contact list full of people I only message when I need something.
The project cycle
1. Pick an idea that is genuinely interesting, forces me to get more technical, and might travel. It has to interest me and give somebody else a reason to care.
2. Build it quickly. Make the central idea work. Skip cosmetic fine-tuning that delays finding out whether anyone wants it.
3. Put the actual thing in front of people. Treat the response as an early signal, then watch whether people use it, return to it, or ask for more. A viral post is a distribution win; it is not enough to prove demand. If it takes off, make a video that shows why it is interesting.
4. Write a technical post. Explain the decisions, the failures, and what I learned. Send it to people who would have something useful to say. Stay in touch.
Given 200 days, a seven-day cycle gives me 28 complete projects. A ten-day cycle gives me 20. A fourteen-day cycle gives me 14, before allowing time between projects. The point is to make more serious attempts, not to produce a graveyard of rushed demos.
If something works unusually well, stay with it. The schedule should help me find that thing, not force me to abandon it for the next launch.
What the attention is for
Would I rather cash out early for less than $1 million, or earn enough trust with exceptional people to raise more than $1 million for something much bigger a year later? If the mission is a generational company, I need to think beyond the immediate payout. Neither outcome is guaranteed, and I should not pretend that ambition makes it so.
Social capital matters because people decide whether to work with me, introduce me, or take a chance on an idea before it looks obvious. I want that trust to come from evidence that I can do the work.
The external branding can stay simple: “I just want to build cool stuff.” Then I need to make things that justify the sentence.
The attention of a few exceptional builders can matter more than approval from a large crowd. I do not need to win every argument or make everyone like me. But making strangers angry is not a strategy either. It can consume the same time I am trying to protect.
Keep the work in charge
I only need one thing to work out really well. Speed gives me more chances to find it, provided each attempt leaves me more capable and better connected than before.
I want to measure a cycle by what I can now build, what I learned about demand, and who I would want to work with again. The post is part of the process. It cannot become the whole process.
Learn in public when there is something worth teaching. Show the work when there is something worth seeing. Then close the tab and get back to it.
Back to the index ↑
I have been in Bangalore for a few months now, and I keep running into the same pattern: people larping a life instead of living it.
Not the fun kind of LARP. I mean the everyday roleplay: founder without a product, researcher without research, operator without operations. Everybody has the vocabulary. Everybody has the vibes. Nobody has a body of work.
It is easy to dismiss as harmless posturing, but it is not harmless. Every hour spent rehearsing an identity is an hour you could have spent building the capabilities that would make the identity true.
Every bit of neuroplasticity you spend learning to perform an identity is plasticity you are not spending on becoming capable. You can train yourself to do the thing, or train yourself to look like the kind of person who does the thing. One compounds. The other decays.
What larping looks like in the wild
Larping is not lying exactly. It is closer to premature narration. You claim a role before you have earned the constraints that come with it.
A builder has a calendar full of trade-offs. A larper has a calendar full of meetings.
A writer has drafts, edits, and a private graveyard of bad paragraphs. A larper has hot takes and a thread schedule.
An investor has a point of view and a record of decisions. A larper has a taste for being near the word ‘deal’.
Why it is so contagious
Bangalore is dense with ambition, which is good. But dense ambition also creates a market for shortcuts: signaling competence instead of acquiring it.
Social media rewards narrative coherence. Communities reward familiarity with the right nouns. Networks reward proximity. All of these can be farmed without doing the work.
And once you say the sentence out loud—‘I’m a founder’, ‘I’m an AI researcher’—your brain starts protecting it. You avoid situations that could reveal you are not that yet. The mask becomes fragile, and then you start spending more energy maintaining it.
The case of larpers: the hidden cost
The main cost is not that other people are fooled. The main cost is that you are.
If you keep repeating the identity, you get a cheap hit of progress without the pain of practice. You begin to confuse recognition with skill.
That is where the neuroplasticity point matters: your brain is always learning something. If you train it on performance, it gets better at performance. If you train it on reality, it gets better at reality.
Larping is a way to spend your adaptability on becoming a convincing character instead of a capable person.
An anti-larping protocol
1. Pick a craft and define output. Not ‘work on my startup’—ship a feature, close a sale, write 1,000 good words, solve a specific technical problem.
2. Reduce audience. If you feel an urge to post, delay it by a week. Use the week to produce something you can only produce by doing real work.
3. Collect receipts privately. Keep a log of what you built, what broke, and what you learned. The log is for you, not for applause.
4. Seek friction. Work that has no resistance is usually just roleplay. Pick tasks that can fail in public because they are real.
5. Let the label arrive late. Titles are a trailing indicator. If the work is real, people will assign the label for you.
A kinder framing
Most larpers are not malicious. They are anxious, ambitious, and surrounded by people who seem ahead. Larping is a coping strategy: it turns uncertainty into a story.
But if you care about becoming dangerous—in the good sense—then you have to stop spending your best learning hours on story.
Use your neuroplasticity somewhere better. Spend it on the work. Become the person quietly. Then talk.

title: Daily — Shubh
text:
Skip to content
← Shubh
02/09/2026
Trying to be honest about the scorecard.
There is a version of success that looks very convincing from a distance: money came in, things moved, nothing fully fell apart. But I have been thinking about the difference between being busy and building a life I actually want to recognise.
Envy is ugly, but it is also information. I do not want to let it turn into self-pity. I want to figure out what it is pointing at.
